payload.rationale: Both sides argued with high skill and sustained direct clash over a single decisive question: should 'greatness' be measured by durable mass-audience devotion (PRO/IMDb) or by professional craft, canon, and influence (CON). CON won the framing war by repeatedly attacking the warrant behind IMDb's #1 ranking (self-selected, recency- and English-skewed popularity, not merit) while stacking convergent professional-consensus evidence: AFI #2, the 1972 Oscar sweep, first-class National Film Registry induction, Sight & Sound, and Ebert's Great Movies essay. PRO mounted a strong, coherent counter-standard (durable global resonance, the National Film Registry as equalizer, AFI Cheers #23, Ebert on Shawshank, the Citizen-Kane-lost-the-Oscar parry) and fought CON to a near-draw on several lines. The round turned on ping 8: PRO alleged CON committed a factual error and asserted Shawshank ranks #72 on AFI's 2007 100 Years...100 Movies list. CON refuted this in the same turn with a cited source, correctly showing Shawshank appears on neither the 1998 nor 2007 AFI Movies list and naming the films the 2007 edition actually added. Under the refute-with-citation rule this both rehabilitated CON and penalized PRO for advancing an uncited falsehood, damaging PRO's credibility on its own chosen authority. CON also neutralized PRO's Citizen Kane analogy by turning it toward Sight & Sound, where The Godfather places and Shawshank is absent. PRO's universality/theme arguments largely stood as conceded ('moving'/'admirable'), but they never overcame CON's craft-and-influence burden case. CON's score is strictly higher on Matter, Clash, and Burden.
payload.persuasion_notes: Principle 3 (refute-a-lie-with-citation) was decisive: PRO's fabricated AFI #72 ranking was contradicted by CON with a same-turn source, so the allegation rebounded against PRO and CON gained credibility. Principle 2 (clash): both engaged directly turn-on-turn, but CON's rebuttals more consistently struck the opponent's warrant rather than restating talking points. Principle 1 (persuasion not truth): judged on defense quality, not on which film is 'really' greater; CON simply defended its standard more cleanly and exposed the weakest link in PRO's. Principle 4 (dropped arguments): PRO's thematic-universality and Ebert-honored-Shawshank points went largely conceded and were credited, keeping PRO competitive and the margin moderate rather than lopsided. Principle 5 invoked only as confirmation, not needed to break a tie since scores differ.
